Vaccination is the act of giving a person (or animal) a vaccine — a specially prepared substance — to protect them from a specific disease. The goal is to make the body ready to fight that disease before it ever actually encounters it.
The core idea: teaching your immune system

Your body has an immune system — a natural defense force that fights off germs like viruses and bacteria. When you catch a disease for the first time, your immune system fights it, but this takes time. During that time, you get sick, sometimes seriously.

Vaccination is a way to train your immune system in advance, without you having to go through the actual disease.

A vaccine introduces something into your body — it could be a weakened or killed version of a germ, a small harmless piece of it, or even just a set of chemical instructions — that teaches your immune system what that germ looks like. Your body then builds antibodies: specialized proteins that know how to target and destroy that specific germ.

If the real germ ever enters your body in the future, your immune system already knows it. It responds fast, often before you even get sick — or at least makes the illness much milder.

The word can refer to:

  • A single event: "The vaccination took only a few seconds." (meaning: the moment a vaccine was administered)
  • The overall process or practice: "Vaccination has saved millions of lives." (meaning: the broader medical practice of using vaccines)
  • A program or campaign: "The government launched a vaccination drive across the country."

So depending on context, it can mean the specific act of injecting a vaccine into one person, or the entire concept of using vaccines as a public health tool.
Types of vaccination (based on how the vaccine works)

There are different kinds of vaccines, and therefore different kinds of vaccination:

  • Live-attenuated vaccination: The vaccine contains a weakened (but living) form of the germ. Example: the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
  • Inactivated vaccination: The vaccine contains a killed version of the germ. Example: some flu vaccines.
  • Subunit vaccination: Only a small, harmless piece of the germ (like a protein from its surface) is used. Example: the hepatitis B vaccine.
  • mRNA vaccination: The vaccine gives your cells temporary chemical instructions to produce a harmless protein that the immune system can learn from. Example: the COVID-19 vaccines from Pfizer and Moderna.
  • Booster vaccination: An additional dose given after the initial one(s) to "remind" or strengthen the immune system's memory. Example: tetanus boosters given every few years.

The word "vaccination" applies to all of these — the type just describes the specific method used.
Why vaccination matters: beyond the individual

Vaccination protects not just the person who receives it, but potentially everyone around them. This is through a concept called herd immunity (also called community immunity):

When a large enough share of a population is vaccinated, a disease can no longer spread easily — because it keeps running into immune people who can't pass it on. This protects vulnerable people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns, the elderly, or people with certain medical conditions.

This is why vaccination is considered one of the most important tools in public health. It has:

  • Eradicated smallpox entirely (the last natural case was in 1977)
  • Brought polio to the edge of elimination worldwide
  • Dramatically reduced deaths from measles, diphtheria, whooping cough, and many other diseases

It helps to know how "vaccination" relates to nearby words:

  • Vaccine (noun): the actual substance — the liquid or preparation that is administered. ("The doctor prepared the vaccine.")
  • Vaccinate (verb): the action of giving a vaccine to someone. ("The nurse will vaccinate the child today.")
  • Vaccination (noun): the act, process, or event of vaccinating. ("The vaccination was quick and painless.")
  • Vaccinated (adjective): describes a person or animal that has received a vaccine. ("She is fully vaccinated.")
  • Vaccinator (noun): a person who administers vaccines.

You will often see "vaccination" used with these words:

  • Routine vaccination — vaccines given as part of a standard schedule (e.g., childhood vaccines)
  • Mandatory/compulsory vaccination — vaccination required by law or policy
  • Mass vaccination — vaccinating a large population quickly, often during an outbreak
  • Vaccination campaign / drive / program — an organized effort to vaccinate many people
  • Vaccination schedule — a planned timetable of which vaccines to give and when
  • Vaccination rate — the percentage of a population that has been vaccinated
  • Childhood vaccination — vaccines administered in early life to protect children
  • Flu vaccination — specifically for influenza

• "The doctor advised annual vaccination against the flu, especially for the elderly."
  • "Mass vaccination campaigns helped bring polio to the brink of extinction."
  • "The school required proof of vaccination before enrollment."
  • "She experienced mild soreness after her vaccination, which was completely normal."
  • "Increasing vaccination rates is key to achieving herd immunity."
  • "A booster vaccination is sometimes needed when immunity fades over time."

Vaccination is the medical act or practice of introducing a vaccine into a person's body to trigger an immune response — training the body to recognize and fight a specific disease without the person having to suffer through it. It protects individuals, shields vulnerable communities through herd immunity, and at the largest scale, has helped humanity control or eliminate some of history's deadliest diseases.
